passage:
Hafsa, you've been angry all week. I can see it from the touchline. Let me tell you something about your old coach Nitin.
When I was sixteen, my father's shop in the market was pulled down for a road-widening scheme. No warning that we understood, no money for months. At school a teacher called me 'shopless boy' as a joke, in front of everyone, and the class laughed. I went home and didn't speak for two days.
At night I found videos online. Young men, older than me, saying exactly what I felt. That the system crushes people like us. That nobody in power cares. That it's not our fault.
I can't tell you the relief. Somebody finally got it. I watched them till three in the morning.
And you know what? Some of what they said was true. The shop was gone. The joke was cruel.
That's why it pulled me in so fast.

qa.q: What happened to Nitin's father's shop?
qa.a: It was pulled down for a road-widening scheme.

qa.q: Why did the videos bring Nitin such relief at sixteen?
qa.a: He was angry and humiliated, and the videos voiced exactly what he felt, so for once he felt understood.

qa.q: What turning point could Hafsa take from Coach Nitin's story at this stage?
qa.a: Hafsa could talk about the anger with a trusted adult like Coach Nitin, instead of looking online for voices that only feed it.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see this week of anger after hearing the story?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel less alone and see that a real hurt can make angry online voices feel like the only ones who understand.

grounding: It shows a teen humiliated by a real loss finding online videos that voice his anger, with the relief of being understood and a grievance partly true.

The electricity board had cut the power again, so Jeevan sat on the steps of the building in Asansol, his phone at eight percent, the only light on the dark stairwell.
That afternoon his father had come home with the envelope from the factory. Laid off, after nineteen years. His mother had cried in the kitchen quietly so they wouldn't hear. And at school, when the tuition fees were called out, Jeevan's name was read twice. Someone in the back row had laughed.
He scrolled. A video came up: a young man shouting that people like his father are used and thrown away, while the rich laugh. Jeevan watched it to the end. Then another.
His friend Anirban messaged: 'u ok? saw ur face in class.'
Jeevan didn't reply. The man in the video understood. His chest felt looser than it had all day. Six percent. He kept watching.

qa.q: How long had Jeevan's father worked at the factory?
qa.a: He had worked there for nineteen years.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan's chest feel looser as he watched the video?
qa.a: He felt relief at being understood, because the video voiced the anger and humiliation he had felt all day.

qa.q: What could help Jeevan at this stage, before the anger grows?
qa.a: Replying to Anirban and talking to a trusted adult about his father's job and the fees could give Jeevan real support instead of an angry feed.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel when that message goes unanswered?
qa.a: Anirban may feel worried and shut out, having noticed Jeevan's face in class but not getting a reply.

grounding: It shows a teen hurt by his father's job loss and humiliation at school finding online videos that voice his anger, bringing relief over a partly true grievance.

passage:
Since his father lost his job at the textile mill in Kanpur, Tanvir had heard the word "retrenchment" more often than his own name. Then, in class, the maths teacher read out his low marks and said, "Your future is a tea stall." The class laughed.
That night, lying on the mattress he shared with his younger brother, Tanvir scrolled. A video popped up: a young man in a dark room, speaking fast. "They closed your father's factory. They laugh at you in school. And nobody says it out loud. I'm saying it."
Tanvir sat up. It was exactly what he felt. Someone finally got it. He watched three more.
His mother, Rehana, called from the kitchen, "Beta, sleep, you have school." He said, "Coming, Ammi," and kept the phone under the blanket, the angry voice in his ear feeling almost like company.

qa.q: What did the maths teacher say to Tanvir?
qa.a: Your future is a tea stall.

qa.q: Why did the video feel like company to Tanvir?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and afraid for his family, so hearing his anger said aloud brought relief, like being understood.

qa.q: What could Rehana or a teacher do at this stage?
qa.a: Acknowledge that the job loss and the teacher's remark were really unfair, and talk with Tanvir about it so a video is not the only thing that seems to understand him.

qa.q: What might Rehana be carrying at the same time?
qa.a: Rehana is likely worried and stretched by the job loss, not knowing how alone and humiliated Tanvir feels.

grounding: A teen hurt by his father's job loss and a teacher's humiliation finds an angry video that voices his partly true grievance, and feels relief.

passage:
"Paper leaked again," Lalit said, dropping his phone on the bench. "Third time. I trained two years for that constable exam, Baljeet. Two years of running at five."
"I know, yaar. My brother too."
"And the news just says 'inquiry ordered'. Every time. Nobody goes to jail."
"It's unfair."
"You know who actually says it? This guy online." Lalit played a clip. A voice shouted, "They sell your seat and then call you lazy. When will you wake up?"
"He's so angry."
"He's right, though! Finally someone's not pretending it's fine." Lalit's eyes were wet, and he wiped them fast. "I watched him till two last night. It's the only time I don't feel stupid."
"Some of what he says is true," Baljeet said slowly. "The leak's real."
"Exactly. It's real."

qa.q: How many times has the paper leaked?
qa.a: Third time.

qa.q: Why does Lalit say the videos are the only time he doesn't feel stupid?
qa.a: He feels cheated and humiliated after two years of training, and the angry voice gives him relief by naming a real injustice.

qa.q: What could Baljeet or an adult do at this stage?
qa.a: Agree the leak is genuinely unfair, stay with Lalit's disappointment, and help him find real routes, like the next exam or a formal complaint, not just angry clips.

qa.q: What might Baljeet be feeling as Lalit plays the clip?
qa.a: Baljeet shares some of the anger but feels uneasy at how intense the voice is, choosing words carefully.

grounding: A teen cheated by a leaked exam finds an online voice for his partly true grievance and feels understood.

passage:
Last year the school dropped me from the debate team for "attitude", when all I'd done was argue back to a teacher who mocked my accent. After that I felt like I was on fire all the time. I'd been the best speaker in my class. Nobody listened when I explained.
That's when the posts found me. An account that said schools and "people in charge" crush anyone who's different, and that the only answer was rage. Every post sounded like my own diary. I remember reading one at midnight and actually crying with relief. Someone understood.
The thing is, part of it was true. What happened at school was unfair.
My brother Tejas noticed I'd stopped eating with the family and was always on my phone, jaw tight. One night he sat on my bed and said, "Tell me what happened with debate. The real version." I'm Deepika, and that was the first time I told anyone.

qa.q: Why was Deepika dropped from the debate team?
qa.a: For 'attitude'.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel reading the post at midnight?
qa.a: Deepika felt a painful relief, crying because the angry words matched a real sense of being wronged and unheard.

qa.q: Why was Tejas's question a good step?
qa.a: Asking for 'the real version' took the grievance seriously and gave Deepika a real person to be understood by, not only the account.

qa.q: What might Tejas have noticed and felt before sitting on the bed?
qa.a: He noticed the missed meals and tight jaw and probably felt worried and protective.

grounding: A teen humiliated at school finds online posts that voice the anger of a partly true grievance, and the relief of feeling understood.

passage:
Note by the class teacher, Class 10B, Friday
Himani has been quieter since the inter-school quiz selection. She topped the trials, but the place went to a student whose parent is on the school committee. I believe she has a real point, and I said so to the coordinator.
This week, in free period, Siddharth mentioned that Himani watches a creator who posts long videos about "rigged systems" and "people like us who never get a chance." Today, in the essay on fairness, she quoted him twice. She looked almost lighter while writing, as if someone finally understood her.
What I did next: I asked Himani to stay back and told her the selection had been unfair and she was right to be angry. I asked what the videos said that felt true. She talked for ten minutes. I have asked the counsellor to meet her next week, and I've called her mother to share what I noticed.

qa.q: Who mentioned the videos Himani watches?
qa.a: Siddharth mentioned that Himani watches a creator who posts long videos about rigged systems.

qa.q: How does Himani seem to feel when she quotes the videos in her essay?
qa.a: She seems relieved and understood, looking almost lighter, because the videos voice the anger she feels about the unfair selection.

qa.q: What turning point does the teacher use, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: The teacher first admits the grievance is real, then listens to what feels true in the videos, which keeps Himani talking instead of pushing her further toward the creator.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about having mentioned the videos?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel a little uneasy about talking behind Himani's back but also relieved that an adult is paying attention.

grounding: Shows a teenager with a partly true grievance finding online content that voices her anger and feeling relieved to be understood.
